section.title: Gethsemane, Arrest, and Peter's Denial
section.sectionRationale: On the Mount of Olives Jesus prays in agony, asking that the cup pass yet surrendering to the Father's will, strengthened by an angel while His disciples sleep. Judas arrives with a crowd and betrays Him with a kiss; Jesus heals the wounded servant and gives Himself to the hour of darkness. As He is led away, Peter denies three times that he knows Him, and the Lord's look breaks his heart. Mocked and beaten through the night, Jesus stands before the Sanhedrin and confesses that from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of God.
section.thesis: In the garden and before His judges Jesus embraces the cup of suffering in perfect surrender to the Father, refusing the sword and healing His enemy, so that even in betrayal, denial, and mockery He goes as the willing, reigning Son of Man to His appointed hour.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the agony and prayer in Gethsemane; the betrayal and arrest; Peter's threefold denial and the Lord's look; and the mocking and the confession before the Sanhedrin.

units.label: The agony in Gethsemane
units.note: not My will, but Yours be done

verses.text: Jesus went out as usual to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed Him.
When He came to the place, He told them, “Pray that you will not enter into {{peirasmos|temptation}}.”
And He withdrew about a stone’s throw beyond them, where He knelt down and prayed,
“Father, if You are willing, take this {{poterion|cup}} from Me. Yet not My {{thelema|will}}, but Yours be done.”
Then an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him.
And in His anguish, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.
When Jesus rose from prayer and returned to the disciples, He found them asleep, exhausted from sorrow.
“Why are you sleeping?” He asked. “Get up and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.”

units.label: The betrayal and arrest
units.note: this hour belongs to the power of darkness

verses.text: While He was still speaking, a crowd arrived, led by the man called Judas, one of the Twelve. He approached Jesus to kiss Him.
But Jesus asked him, “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?”
Those around Jesus saw what was about to happen and said, “Lord, should we strike with our swords?”
And one of them struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his right ear.
But Jesus answered, “No more of this!” And He touched the man’s ear and healed him.
Then Jesus said to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders who had come for Him, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as you would against an outlaw?
Every day I was with you in the temple courts, and you did not lay a hand on Me. But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.”

units.label: Peter's denial
units.note: the Lord turned and looked at Peter

verses.text: Then they seized Jesus, led Him away, and took Him into the house of the high priest. And Peter followed at a distance.
When those present had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.
A servant girl saw him seated in the firelight and looked intently at him. “This man also was with Him,” she said.
But Peter denied it. “Woman, I do not know Him,” he said.
A short time later, someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.”
About an hour later, another man insisted, “Certainly this man was with Him, for he too is a Galilean.”
“Man, I do not know what you are talking about,” Peter replied. And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.
And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the word that the Lord had spoken to him: “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.”
And he went outside and wept bitterly.

units.label: The mocking and the Sanhedrin
units.note: from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of God

verses.text: The men who were holding Jesus began to mock Him and beat Him.
They blindfolded Him and kept demanding, “Prophesy! Who hit You?”
And they said many other blasphemous things against Him.
At daybreak the council of the elders of the people, both the chief priests and scribes, met together. They led Jesus into their Sanhedrin and said,
“If You are the {{christos|Christ}}, tell us.” Jesus answered, “If I tell you, you will not believe.
And if I ask you a question, you will not answer.
But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”
So they all asked, “Are You then the Son of God?” He replied, “You say that I am.”
“Why do we need any more testimony?” they declared. “We have heard it for ourselves from His own lips.”

peirasmos.gloss: Temptation, testing, trial. Twice Jesus tells the disciples to pray not to enter into temptation, for the hour of testing is upon them all. He Himself faces the ultimate trial in the garden and overcomes it by prayer and surrender, while they sleep and soon fall, one to denial. Prayer is the appointed guard against the coming test.

poterion.gloss: Cup. In the prophets the cup is the cup of God's wrath against sin. Jesus asks the Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me, then drinks it in obedience. The cup He shrinks from and yet accepts is the suffering of bearing sin and judgment in His people's place.

thelema.gloss: Will, desire, purpose. Not My will, but Yours be done is the heart of Gethsemane and the reversal of Eden's grasping. The Son surrenders His own recoiling will to the Father's saving purpose, and in that obedience our salvation is secured. It is the prayer He taught His disciples, lived out in agony.

christos.gloss: Christ, Messiah, the Anointed One. The council demands to know if Jesus is the Christ, and He answers by declaring that the Son of Man will be seated at God's right hand, claiming a divine, reigning messiahship far beyond their categories. His confession, made under judgment, is the truth for which they condemn Him and the truth by which we are saved.

basic.context: Jesus goes to the Mount of Olives and tells the disciples to pray not to fall into temptation. Alone, He kneels and prays that if the Father is willing, the cup would pass, yet surrenders, not My will but Yours be done. An angel strengthens Him, and in anguish His sweat falls like drops of blood, while the disciples sleep from sorrow. Judas arrives with a crowd and betrays Him with a kiss; when a disciple cuts off the servant's ear, Jesus says no more of this and heals him, then gives Himself to the hour of darkness. Peter follows at a distance, warms himself at the fire, and three times denies knowing Jesus. The rooster crows, the Lord turns and looks at him, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly. Through the night Jesus is mocked and beaten, and at daybreak He tells the Sanhedrin that the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of God, confessing Himself the Christ and Son of God.
basic.hermeneutics: Gethsemane is the interpretive center: Jesus' surrender of His will secures the salvation His death accomplishes. The arrest, denial, and trial then unfold against this obedience, contrasting His steadfast faithfulness with the disciples' sleep, Peter's denial, and the leaders' blasphemy, while His confession reveals who is truly on trial.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus warns of peirasmos, the coming temptation, and meets His own by prayer. He asks the Father to remove the poterion, the cup of wrath, yet yields with not My thelema, My will, but Yours. And before the council He is asked whether He is the christos, and answers by claiming the Son of Man's seat at God's right hand.
basic.typology: The cup of wrath from the prophets is drunk by Christ in the sinner's place. His surrender in the garden reverses Adam's grasping in Eden. The Son of Man seated at God's right hand fulfills Daniel and Psalm 110, revealing the condemned prisoner as the coming Judge.
basic.christ: Jesus is the obedient Son who drinks the cup He dreads, the King who will not be defended by the sword and heals His captor's servant, and the Son of Man who confesses His coming enthronement even as He is condemned. His faithfulness where Adam and the disciples failed is the ground of salvation.
basic.god: God's will is the saving purpose to which the Son yields, and God sends an angel to strengthen Him. God ordains the hour of darkness without being its author, and God will vindicate His Son by seating Him at His right hand. The Father's will and the Son's obedience together accomplish redemption.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 51 speaks of the cup of God's wrath. Psalm 110 seats the Lord at God's right hand. Daniel 7 gives the Son of Man's dominion. Hebrews 5 says Jesus learned obedience through what He suffered, with loud cries and tears.
basic.oneStory: In the garden the second Adam surrenders His will to the Father where the first Adam grasped, and He drinks the cup of wrath for His people. Betrayed, denied, and mocked, He goes willingly to the cross as the reigning Son of Man, so the story turns on His obedience, the hinge on which our salvation swings.

context.literary:
Luke 22:39 to 71 is a single night told in four scenes, and the scenes are stitched together by repeated words. 'Pray that you will not enter into temptation' stands at the head of the garden scene, verse 40, and again at its close, verse 46, so that the whole prayer is wrapped in a command to the disciples. Their sleeping, and Peter's three denials, are the failure of exactly that command. The kiss of verses 47 to 48 and the fire of verses 55 to 56 are both set against a darkness that Jesus names, 'the power of darkness,' verse 53.

There is a deliberate overlap between the second and third scenes. Verse 54 says they led Jesus away and that Peter followed at a distance, and the narrator then shows Peter in the courtyard, verses 55 to 62, before returning to Jesus, verses 63 to 71. Luke keeps both men in view as if cutting between two rooms: in one a disciple is denying Him, and in the other He is being mocked. The only moment the two lines touch is verse 61, 'the Lord turned and looked at Peter,' which is the hinge of the whole chapter.

The scene with the council forms a sharp contrast with the prayer. In the garden Jesus asks the Father and is silent before men. In the Sanhedrin He is asked directly and speaks at last, and what He says, verse 69, is the first statement in Luke of His present enthronement. Luke has no night trial before Caiaphas. He reports only a morning meeting at daybreak, verse 66, and so the whole sequence of mockery by the guards, verses 63 to 65, comes before the hearing, as a foretaste.

The council puts two questions to Him, 'Are You the Christ?' and then 'Are You then the Son of God?' Luke separates what other accounts compress, and lets the answer to the first, the seat at God's right hand, make the second unavoidable. The last line, 'we have heard it for ourselves from His own lips,' closes the chapter on an irony: the council convicts Him on His own words, which are in fact the truth.
context.historical:
The Mount of Olives rises east of the temple across the Kidron valley, and Gethsemane, a name connected with an olive press, was a grove on its slope. Luke says Jesus went there 'as usual,' verse 39, and Luke 21:37 has already said He spent his nights on the mountain. Judas therefore knew exactly where to bring the crowd, and it explains the leaders' plan to take Him there, away from the festival crowd, verse 6. David had once crossed the Kidron and climbed the same hill weeping, betrayed by a trusted counsellor, 2 Samuel 15:23 and 15:30 to 31.

The company that arrives is a mixed force. The 'chief priests, temple officers, and elders,' verse 52, are temple authorities. The temple officers served as the temple's police under the priests, which explains the high priest's servant who is wounded. The kiss was an ordinary greeting between a disciple and his teacher, and thus an ideal means of marking the man in the dark. 'Swords and clubs' is the equipment of a posse seizing an outlaw, a word for a bandit, and Jesus' retort in verse 52 points out that He had taught openly every day, and no hand was laid on Him.

The high priest's house had a courtyard with a fire, and servants and guards sat about it on a cold spring night. A servant girl, a bystander, and a man a little later recognised Peter as Galilean, verse 59. Galileans were known for a distinctive way of speaking, a feature the other Gospels draw on. The three questions are spread over about an hour, so the third is no snap reaction but a settled refusal.

The Sanhedrin that meets 'at daybreak' is the ruling council in Jerusalem. It could hear a case, but had to hand over a capital sentence to the Roman governor, which is why chapter 23 begins at Pilate's door. The charge of blasphemy depended on a claim to share God's honour, and the title 'Son of God' as a claim to a unique relationship with Him would be heard in that light.
context.canonical:
Gethsemane gathers a number of Old Testament pictures. The cup is an image of God's judgment in Isaiah 51:17, where Jerusalem has 'drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury,' in Jeremiah 25:15, where the nations are made to drink 'the wine of wrath,' and in Psalm 75:8, where the wicked drink it 'to the dregs.' Isaiah 51:22 then promises that the cup of staggering will be taken away from God's people, and in Gethsemane the same cup is taken up by the Son. John records Jesus' words on the same night, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11.

Hebrews reads the garden as a window into the Son's earthly life. 'He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears,' and 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:7 to 8. The command to pray against temptation echoes the Lord's Prayer, Luke 11:4, and the long conflict with the tempter that began in the wilderness, when he 'left Him until an opportune time,' Luke 4:13. Paul sets the obedience of this night against the first man's disobedience, 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19.

The council scene draws on two psalms and a vision. Psalm 110:1, 'Sit at My right hand,' is the text Jesus had pressed on His opponents in Luke 20:41 to 44, and the BSB footnote notes it at Luke 22:69. The title Son of Man comes from Daniel 7:13. Stephen, standing before the same council, will see 'the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God,' Acts 7:55 to 56, and Revelation 1:7 completes the picture with the One who 'is coming with the clouds.'

Peter's failure is itself taken up. Jesus had warned that whoever denies Him before men 'will be denied before the angels of God,' Luke 12:9. After the resurrection He asks Peter three times, 'Do you love Me?' John 21:15 to 17, and the restored apostle later writes of One who, 'when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see a Jesus who is neither swept along nor trapped. The garden is the proof: the shortest path out of suffering is available in prayer, and the whole scene is a choice made in full awareness. By recording the anguish, the strengthening angel and the sweat falling to the ground, Luke refuses to make the Lord's obedience look easy. The cross is chosen by someone who feels what it costs.

He wants them, too, to see how a disciple fails and is kept. Peter's denial is told in unsparing detail, with the three questions, the three answers and the look. But the account is immediately followed by the sentence 'he went outside and wept bitterly,' and Luke has already told us why Peter will come back: 'I have prayed for you,' verse 32. A church that included people who had once run away needed to hear that a denier could be a restored shepherd.

Finally he means the readers to hear the confession before the council as a claim they too must answer. The man being tried says that from now on He is seated at the right hand of the power of God. The judges are being warned that the roles are reversed. Luke's readers, who were being tried before their own councils, were meant to take heart: the Judge of the world had once stood where they stood.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The garden prayer is a unique moment in the Son's saving work. No one else drinks the cup of God's wrath on behalf of others, and the reader is not asked to share in the atonement. But the prayer is also a pattern. 'Pray that you will not enter into temptation' is a plain command, given twice, and the manner of the prayer, honest about the fear and yielding at the end, 'not My will, but Yours be done,' is offered as a way of praying under pressure. It is neither stoic nor rebellious.

The sword is described and corrected. A disciple strikes the servant, and Jesus says 'No more of this!' and heals the wound. The scene does not say that the kingdom advances by force or that Christians must never use force in any circumstance, such as protecting a child. It does say that the cause of Christ is not to be defended by cutting off an enemy's ear.

Peter's denial is a warning and not a model, and Jesus' silence and bearing before the council is a description of His unique mission rather than a rule that believers must never defend themselves in court. Paul appeals to his rights as a citizen, Acts 25:11. What does carry over is Jesus' truthfulness: when asked who He is, He tells the truth, even at the cost of His life.

debates.question: What is the cup Jesus asks the Father to remove?

views.label: The cup of divine wrath against sin
views.case: In the prophets the cup is God's judgment poured out on sin. Jesus recoils not merely from physical death but from bearing the wrath due His people, drinking the cup of judgment in their place. His agony reflects the horror of becoming sin-bearer, and His acceptance secures atonement.

views.label: The whole ordeal of suffering and death
views.case: Some understand the cup more broadly as the entire experience of betrayal, torture, and crucifixion that lay before Him. On this reading His anguish is the fully human dread of a horrific death, met and mastered by trust in the Father.

debates.bearing: Either way the garden reveals the real cost of the cross and the depth of Jesus' obedience; His surrender, not My will but Yours, is what carries Him to drink it for us.

debates.question: Why does Jesus answer the Sanhedrin as He does about the Son of Man?

views.label: A deliberate claim to divine, reigning messiahship
views.case: By fusing Daniel 7 and Psalm 110, Jesus claims to be the Son of Man who will sit at God's right hand and come in judgment. It is a confession of a messiahship far higher than a mere national deliverer, which the council rightly hears as a claim to share God's throne, and so condemns as blasphemy.

views.label: A turning of the tables on His judges
views.case: Jesus reframes the trial: though He stands condemned before them now, from now on they will face Him as the enthroned Son of Man. The One being judged is in truth the coming Judge, so His answer is both confession and warning to the court.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that Jesus confesses His true identity under oath: the condemned prisoner is the Christ, the Son of God, and the Son of Man soon to be seated in power at God's right hand.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 44 says that Jesus was en agonia, 'in anguish.' The word agonia belongs to the vocabulary of the contest and the arena, a struggle of the whole person. In the same verse Luke says He prayed ektenesteron, 'more earnestly,' a comparative of a word meaning stretched out, so the prayer is strained to its limit. The sweat 'became like drops of blood,' hosei thromboi haimatos. Luke says 'like' and not 'was,' and the word thromboi means clots or heavy drops, so the picture is of sweat thick and falling, in a way that the Gospel offers as an image and not a medical claim. The BSB footnote warns that some manuscripts do not include verses 43 and 44, so the passage is not used as the sole proof of any point, and the central doctrine of Gethsemane stands on verses 41 to 42 and on the other Gospels.

The disciples are found asleep koimomenous apo tes lypes, 'from grief,' lype being sorrow or heaviness. Only Luke gives the reason, and it takes the edge off the rebuke. They were not careless but crushed, and yet the command of verse 46 stands. In verse 41 He 'withdrew,' apespasthe, a verb that can mean being drawn or torn away, and the distance is 'a stone's throw,' lithou bolen. He needs to be at a distance but within reach of their sight.

The kiss gets two words that matter. In verse 47 Judas approaches 'to kiss,' philesai, from the verb phileo, to love as a friend, and in verse 48 Jesus asks about philemati, 'with a kiss.' The sign of friendship is the instrument of betrayal. Jesus addresses him by name and speaks of the Son of Man, which makes the question a last appeal.

Verse 51 holds a short Greek phrase that is hard to render, eate heos toutou, which could mean 'No more of this,' or 'Let it go this far.' It is addressed either to the disciples, telling them to stop, or to the captors, asking leave to heal. The healing, iasato, is told only by Luke, the verb that fits the physician of the Gospel's reputation and the healer of the whole Gospel. Jesus ends the violence by undoing its damage.

In verse 53 He calls the hour 'the power of darkness,' hē exousia tou skotous. Exousia is authority, the same word used of Jesus' own authority elsewhere in Luke, so darkness is permitted a delegated authority for a time. Compare Luke 4:13, 'an opportune time.' It is given and it is limited.

Peter's story has several verbs worth noticing. The servant girl 'looked intently,' atenisasa, verse 56, and the Lord 'looked at' Peter, eneblepsen, verse 61, a different verb for a long, direct look. Peter says 'I do not know Him,' and Luke uses a form of arneomai, 'deny,' the very verb of Luke 12:9, where Jesus warns about denying Him before men. And Peter 'wept bitterly,' eklausen pikros, and the adverb pikros gives the weeping its sharp edge.

In verse 65 the men mock Him with many 'blasphemous' things, blasphemountes, which is the same word the council will use in the other Gospels against Him. The irony is that the real blasphemy is in the mockers' mouths, since the one they blindfold and bid to 'Prophesy!' is the prophet whose words just came true about Peter.

In verse 69 the 'right hand of the power of God' uses dynamis, power, as a name for God, a reverent way of speaking. And 'You say that I am,' verse 70, is hymeis legete hoti ego eimi in the Greek, and it is neither a refusal nor a plain yes. It lets them hear the truth in their own words.

typology.type: The cup of wrath, Isaiah 51:17 and Luke 22:42
typology.fulfillment: In Isaiah, Jerusalem has drunk from the LORD's hand the cup of His fury and drained it to the dregs, and God then promises to take it away, Isaiah 51:17 and 51:22. The cup is the symbol of judgment upon a guilty people. In Gethsemane Jesus asks whether it can pass and then takes it. Paul says God 'made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Isaiah's promise that the cup will never be drunk again is fulfilled because He drank it. The type falls short in that Jerusalem drank for its own sin, whereas Christ drinks for sins that were not His.

typology.type: David climbing the Mount of Olives, 2 Samuel 15:23 and 15:30
typology.fulfillment: David the anointed king crossed the Kidron and went up the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered, betrayed by his own counsellor Ahithophel, 2 Samuel 15:30 to 31. Jesus the son of David crosses the same valley, John 18:1, goes to the same hill and is betrayed by a companion who shared His table, as Psalm 41:9 describes. The correspondence is a righteous king rejected by a trusted friend. The escalation lies in the outcome: David was driven out to save his throne, while Jesus gives up His life and rises as King. The type fails because David fled the conspiracy and Jesus went to meet it.

typology.type: The Servant who offers His back, Isaiah 50:6
typology.fulfillment: The Servant says 'I offered My back to those who struck Me' and 'I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle,' and says 'I have set My face like flint,' Isaiah 50:6 to 7. Luke's account of the guards who blindfold and beat Jesus, verses 63 to 65, is the enactment of this, and so is the resolve with which He went to Jerusalem, Luke 9:51. Peter would later write that He 'did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. The Servant's trust that he would not be put to shame was met by the resurrection. The type is surpassed because the Servant here suffers for others and not only for faithfulness.

typology.type: The obedient Son in the garden, Genesis 3 and Luke 22:42
typology.fulfillment: Adam was placed in a garden with every provision and chose his own will against God's word. Jesus enters another garden under pressure and says 'not My will, but Yours be done.' Paul sets the two against each other, 'through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19. Hebrews adds that He 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8. The pattern is of a representative head, and in Christ the correspondence overturns the first. It is also unlike Adam in that the second Adam's obedience reaches all the way to death.

study.christ:
The garden shows Christ as the truly human Son. He feels fear, asks that the cup pass, and needs an angel's strength. Hebrews says that 'we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15, and the Gethsemane scene is the proof that this is not a figure of speech. He is not a distant deity moving through a role. The one who will intercede for us knows what it is to pray in terror.

He is also the Son who obeys. The prayer is 'if You are willing,' and the end is 'Yours be done.' All of Luke's Gospel has been moving to this point, from the boy who must be in His Father's house to the man who 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem,' Luke 9:51. The obedience of this hour is the obedience on which our salvation hangs, the second Adam's answer to the first, Romans 5:19. He is the one who does not turn back, where Isaiah's Servant 'set His face like flint,' Isaiah 50:7.

He is the King who will not be defended by force. When the disciples ask, 'Lord, should we strike with our swords?' He answers by healing the wounded man. John records Him saying that His kingdom is not of this world, or His servants would fight, John 18:36, and Matthew adds that He could call on legions of angels, Matthew 26:53. He lays down His power by choice. The healing of the servant's ear is an act of kindness to an enemy performed in the moment of His own arrest, a preview of 'Father, forgive them' in the next chapter.

He is the Lord who looks at Peter. Nothing in the denial surprises Him, since He had said it, and the look is not a look of condemnation, since He had also said 'I have prayed for you.' It is the look that brings Peter to remembrance and then to tears. In John 21 He gives Peter three questions for three denials and restores him. Christ is the shepherd who retrieves what is lost, the one who stood alone so that the denier could be taken back.

He is the Son of Man who is enthroned. The prisoner in the council room declares that 'from now on' He is seated at the right hand of the power of God. Psalm 110:1, which He had put to His opponents in Luke 20:41 to 44, is now claimed as His own, and Daniel 7:13 stands behind the title Son of Man. The one who is blindfolded and told to prophesy is the one who sees the end. When He says 'You say that I am,' He is confessing His identity, though He knows it will cost Him His life.

He is also the one who takes the cup in our place. The cup of wrath of Isaiah and Jeremiah is drunk by the Son so that His people do not have to drink it. In Gethsemane we see the price before the cross itself.

A word of care keeps this honest. The ear, the servant, the fire and the rooster are real events, not allegories, and the sleeping disciples are not a hidden picture of Christ's enemies. The weight rests on the prayer, the arrest and the confession.
study.god:
The garden shows a God who is Father. Jesus' prayer begins with the single word 'Father,' and everything in the scene rests on that relationship. The Son asks, and the Father is the one who decides, who sends an angel to strengthen, and who gives the cup. That is a startling picture of the Father's will: He does not spare the Son, yet He does not abandon Him in the hour. The strength given by the angel is the Father's sustaining presence in the middle of the ordeal.

He is a God whose will is good and costly. 'If You are willing' acknowledges that the cup is the Father's will, and the Son's 'Yours be done' accepts it as good. Peter says in Acts that Jesus was 'delivered up by God's set plan and foreknowledge,' Acts 2:23, and the early church prays that Herod and Pilate 'carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand,' Acts 4:27 to 28. Yet the scene never lets human guilt dissolve. Judas comes with a kiss, the leaders come with clubs, and the guards mock. God's plan and human responsibility sit together.

He is a God who limits evil. Jesus calls this hour 'the power of darkness,' and darkness has real authority for a time, but it is a delegated authority with a boundary, much as it was with Job. Satan could sift, but not without a request, and not beyond a prayer.

He is just and merciful at once. The cup is a cup of judgment, and the Son must drink it, because God does not wave sin away. Yet the same God has chosen that the judgment should fall on His own Son and not on His people. Justice and mercy are not balanced against each other in this scene but joined. Isaiah had said of the cup, 'you will never drink again,' Isaiah 51:22, and the reason is now visible.

He is a God who strengthens in weakness. The angel appears only after the prayer of surrender and in answer to it. God does not remove the cup but sends the strength to drink it. The same pattern lies behind Peter's later restoration and behind Paul's comfort that God is faithful and will not allow testing beyond what we can bear.

He is a God who has sovereign authority over the judges themselves. The council believes it sits in judgment, but the accused tells them the real order, that He will be seated at God's right hand. The whole night, in which God seems silent, is under His rule.

Worship in this light begins with awe at the Father's costly will and the Son's costly obedience, and it moves to trust, because the God who gave His Son in the garden will not abandon those who pray in their own.

crossReferences.note: Matthew's garden scene adds that Jesus took Peter and the sons of Zebedee, said 'My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death,' and prayed 'let this cup pass from Me.' Luke's shorter account gains from this: the anguish is not a poetic touch but part of the recorded testimony.

The writer remembers the garden: 'He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears,' and 'He learned obedience from what He suffered.' It reads the prayer as part of the Son's training as a perfect high priest, and shows that Luke 22:44 was long understood as a moment of real struggle.

Jerusalem has drunk 'the cup of His fury' and drained it to the dregs. It is the Old Testament source of the cup that Jesus asks to be removed. Isaiah 51:22 then promises that the cup will be taken from the people's hands, which is what Gethsemane makes possible.

The LORD gives Jeremiah 'the cup of the wine of wrath' to make the nations drink. Together with Psalm 75:8 it shows that the cup in Scripture is the cup of divine judgment, which makes the Son's dread of it intelligible and gives weight to His choice.

John names the swordsman as Simon Peter and the servant as Malchus, and gives Jesus' words, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' This links the arrest directly back to the garden prayer and shows the answer was already settled.

David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered, after hearing that Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy. The king betrayed by a trusted friend and the same hill and valley make a deliberate echo, which the Gospels hear in Jesus' own night.

Jesus had said that those who confess Him before men He will confess before the angels, and those who deny Him will be denied. Peter's three denials make the warning concrete, and the grace of verse 32 and John 21 shows that denial need not be the last word.

The risen Jesus asks Peter three times, 'Do you love Me?' and gives him the charge to feed His sheep. The triple question answers the triple denial. It is the full restoration of the man who wept bitterly, and it shows the prayer of Luke 22:32 answered.

'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool.' Jesus had asked how David's son could also be David's Lord, Luke 20:41 to 44. In Luke 22:69 He claims the seat for Himself, making the psalm the basis of His answer to the council.

One like a son of man approaches the Ancient of Days and receives dominion. Jesus' favourite self-description comes from here, and in the council it is joined to Psalm 110. Together the texts make the claim that the council is judging the one who will judge them.

Stephen, on trial before the same body, sees 'the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.' It shows the confession of Luke 22:69 confirmed by a witness and shows that the Lord now stands to welcome His servant.

We have a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses, tempted in every way yet without sin. The garden is the clearest scene in the Gospels where this sympathy is seen at work, since the Lord prays under the pressure of real temptation.

study.oneStory:
Gethsemane is where the story's oldest problem is met head on. In one garden the first man listened to a voice that questioned God's word, took what was forbidden, and brought exile and death. In another garden, at night, the Son of God hears the same temptation in its sharpest form, to avoid the cost, and chooses the Father's will. Everything that went wrong in Genesis 3 turns on this moment. Paul sees the two gardens as the two heads of humanity, and Romans 5 draws out the consequence: where the one man's disobedience made many sinners, the other man's obedience makes many righteous.

The night also gathers the whole story of covenant failure. The disciples sleep and run, Peter denies, Judas betrays, the leaders conspire, and a Gentile governor will soon give in. All the actors of the human story are shown at their weakest, and the one faithful person is the one who is arrested. This is how the covenant is kept: not by a people who hold on, but by a Mediator who does. The cup of wrath of Isaiah and Jeremiah, the sifting of Job, the Servant of Isaiah 50 and the rejected king of Samuel all meet in His hands.

What follows depends on this scene. Without Gethsemane there is no willing sacrifice, and without the healed ear there is no picture of a kingdom that does not advance by the sword. Without the look at Peter there is no restored apostle to strengthen his brothers, and without the answer to the council there is no enthroned Son of Man to be seen by Stephen and John. The church that Acts describes will rise on this night's work, with a fallen but forgiven Peter at its head.

And the story ends where the council's test is reversed. The one who was blindfolded and told to prophesy will be seen by every eye, Revelation 1:7. The cup He drank is gone for good, and the garden that began with a closed way ends with a tree of life and open gates. The people who are in Him have been spared the cup, and they follow the pattern of the night as they pray, 'not My will, but Yours be done,' in a world that is still dark but already beaten.

quiz.q: How does Jesus pray in Gethsemane?

options.text: He asks the Father to take the cup if He is willing, yet surrenders, not My will but Yours be done.
options.note: Luke 22:42 holds together the plea and the full surrender to the Father's will.

options.text: He asks that the cup of suffering be taken from Him.
options.note: True, but it omits the decisive surrender, not My will but Yours be done.

options.text: He calmly accepts His fate without any struggle.
options.note: His prayer is one of real anguish, sweat like blood, not detached calm.

options.text: He asks the Father to destroy His enemies.
options.note: He prays about the cup and surrenders to the Father's will, not for vengeance.

quiz.q: How does Jesus respond to the sword at His arrest?

options.text: He says 'No more of this' and heals the servant whose ear was cut off.
options.note: Luke 22:51 shows Jesus halting the violence and healing His captor's servant.

options.text: He tells the disciples to stop fighting.
options.note: True, but it omits that He healed the wounded servant, mercy to His enemy.

options.text: He allows the disciples to defend Him with swords.
options.note: The opposite; He forbids further violence and undoes the harm done.

options.text: He calls down angels to strike the crowd.
options.note: He surrenders to the hour of darkness rather than resisting by force.

quiz.q: What happens after Peter denies Jesus three times?

options.text: The rooster crows, the Lord turns and looks at Peter, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.
options.note: Luke 22:60-62 records the crowing, the Lord's look, and Peter's bitter weeping.

options.text: Peter remembers Jesus' words and is filled with grief.
options.note: True, but it omits the piercing detail of the Lord turning to look at him.

options.text: Peter immediately confesses Jesus before the crowd.
options.note: He weeps in private repentance; he does not at once confess Christ openly.

options.text: Peter feels no remorse for his denial.
options.note: He weeps bitterly, deeply grieved by his failure.

quiz.q: What does Jesus confess before the Sanhedrin?

options.text: That from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.
options.note: Luke 22:69 is the climactic claim to divine, reigning messiahship.

options.text: That He is the Christ and the Son of God.
options.note: True from their questions and His reply, but it omits the specific claim to the throne at God's right hand.

options.text: That He is merely a teacher sent from God.
options.note: He claims far more, a seat at the right hand of God's power.

options.text: That He is not the Christ at all.
options.note: He affirms His identity, which is why they condemn Him.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus tell the disciples to pray in the garden?

options.text: So that they will not enter into temptation, the hour of testing about to fall on them.
options.note: Luke 22:40,46 gives the reason: prayer against the coming temptation.

options.text: So that they would stay awake and alert with Him.
options.note: True in effect, but the stated purpose is to be kept from falling into temptation.

options.text: So that they could ask God to spare Jesus from arrest.
options.note: The prayer He commands is for themselves against temptation, not to prevent His arrest.

options.text: Because prayer was simply their evening habit.
options.note: He gives a specific, urgent reason: the coming hour of testing.

questions: Jesus surrendered His will with, not My will but Yours be done. Where is God asking you to yield a desire you are gripping tightly, and what makes that surrender hard?
In His deepest agony Jesus prayed, while the disciples slept. When sorrow or exhaustion weighs on you, do you turn to prayer or drift into a spiritual sleep?
Jesus healed the ear of the man sent to arrest Him. How does His mercy toward an enemy challenge the way you respond to those who wrong you?
The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and it broke him. Have you known that kind of look from Christ, grieved and yet loving, that leads to repentance rather than despair?
Standing condemned, Jesus confessed the truth of who He is. Where are you tempted to stay silent about Christ when honesty would be costly?

translationNotes.note: Some early manuscripts do not include the verses about the strengthening angel and the sweat like drops of blood. The BSB retains them; they vividly convey the reality of Jesus' agony and the Father's provision of strength.
'This cup' draws on the prophetic image of the cup of God's wrath against sin. Jesus prays for its removal yet surrenders to drink it, bearing the judgment due His people.

Jesus fuses Daniel 7:13 and Psalm 110:1, claiming that the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of God's power. The council hears this as a claim to share God's throne and condemns it as blasphemy.
